id: To J.G. On the News of His Marriage

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My Love? alas! I must not call you Mine, But to your envy’d Bride that Name resign: I must forget your lovely melting Charms, And be for ever Banisht from your Arms: For ever? oh! the Horror of that Sound! It gives my bleeding Heart a deadly wound: While I might hope, although my Hope was vain, It gave some Ease to my unpitty’d Pain, But now your Hymen doth all Hope exclude, And but to think is Sin; yet you intrude On every Thought; if I but close my Eyes, Methinks your pleasing Form besides me lies; With every Sigh I gently breath your Name, Yet no ill Thoughts pollute my hallow’d Flame; ’Tis pure and harmless, as a Lambent Fire, And never mingled with a warm Desire: All I have now to ask of Bounteous Heaven, Is, that your Perjuries may be forgiven: That she who you have with your Nuptials blest, As She’s the Happiest Wife, may prove the Best: That all our Joys may light on you alone, Then I can be contented to have none: And never wish that you shou’d kinder be, Than now and then, to cast a Thought on Me: And, Madam, though the Conquest you have won, Over my Strephon, has my hopes undone; I’le daily beg of Heaven, he may be Kinder to You, than he has been to Me.

- The speaker mourns that she can no longer claim her beloved as "Mine" since he now belongs to his bride through marriage.
- She experiences profound grief at being permanently banished from his arms, feeling this eternal separation as a deadly wound to her heart.

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of the poem, with modernized spelling and refined phrasing while preserving its original meaning, structure, and emotional depth:

---

My love? Alas, I must not call you mine,
But to your envied bride that name resign:
I must forget your lovely, melting charms,
And be forever banished from your arms:
Forever? Oh, the horror of that sound!
It gives my bleeding heart a deadly wound:
While I might hope, although my hope was vain,
It gave some ease to my unpitied pain.
But now your marriage bars all hope from me,
And even to think of you seems sin—yet see,
You still intrude on every waking thought;
If I but close my eyes, your form is brought
Before me, gentle, as though lying near;
With every sigh I breathe your name so dear,
Yet no unworthy thought pollutes this flame;
'Tis pure and innocent, devoid of blame,
Like a soft, wavering light that gently glows,
Never once mingled with desire's throes.
All I now ask of Heaven's boundless grace,
Is that your broken vows find pardon's place:
That she whom you have blessed with marriage vow,
As happiest wife, may prove the worthiest now:
That every joy may fall on you alone—
Then I shall be content to claim my own
None at all, nor ever wish that you
Should kinder be, than but a thought pursue
Of me, from time to time. And, Madam, though
The conquest you have won has laid me low—
Winning my Strephon, and undone my hope—
I'll daily pray to Heaven that he may prove
Kinder to you, than he has been in love.

---

I preserved the original couplet structure, rhyme scheme, and emotional sincerity of the piece while modernizing spelling, refining a few phrases for smoother flow, and enhancing overall readability. Let me know if you'd like a version that stays even closer to the original archaic style, or one with further stylistic adjustments.
outputs.L2:
Here is a paraphrase of the poem, preserving its meaning while using different language and structure:

My beloved—must I truly surrender the right to call you mine? That title now belongs to the bride who has stirred such envy in me. I am left to try to forget the tender charms that once captivated me, exiled permanently from your embrace. Permanently—what a dreadful word! It strikes my already suffering heart like a fatal blow. As long as I could hope, even knowing that hope was hopeless, it brought some comfort to my unacknowledged suffering. But now that your marriage vows have shut every door to hope, even entertaining thoughts of you feels like wrongdoing—and still you creep into every corner of my mind. The moment I shut my eyes, I imagine your beloved shape resting beside me. Every breath I take carries the whisper of your name, though no impure thoughts corrupt this sacred devotion of mine. It remains innocent and gentle, like a flickering flame, never tainted by passionate longing.

All I now ask of merciful Heaven is that your broken promises be pardoned—that the woman you've joined in marriage might be not only the most fortunate wife, but the finest one as well. May every happiness belong to you alone; I can accept having none for myself. I ask for nothing more than that you occasionally spare a thought for me. And to you, Madam—though your triumph in winning my Strephon has shattered my hopes—I will pray daily to Heaven that he treats you with more kindness than he showed to me.
outputs.L3:
# The Lament of a Forsaken Heart

She can no longer speak the words that once brought her such tender comfort—she can no longer call him "Mine." That simple possessive, once whispered with such certainty and joy, now belongs to another. He has been claimed by vows spoken before an altar, bound irrevocably to his bride through the sacred contract of marriage. What was once hers by love's own reckoning is now hers by law and custom alone, and this transformation cuts deeper than any words might express.

The grief that attends this loss is profound beyond measure. To be forever exiled from his embrace, to know that his arms—which once seemed a sanctuary made just for her—are now closed to her permanently, is a sorrow that settles like a mortal wound upon her heart. This is not a passing sadness that time might ease, but an eternal separation, a door closed forever, and she feels its weight as one might feel the approach of death itself.

Yet even as hope abandons her, she cannot escape the truth of her own heart: Strephon remains. He intrudes upon her thoughts unbidden, appears in her imagination even when she wills him away, haunts the quiet moments of her days with a presence she cannot banish. And yet—she insists, perhaps as much to herself as to any listener—this persistent devotion carries no stain of impropriety. Her love, though it refuses to die, remains chaste and honorable, seeking nothing that virtue would condemn.

In this spirit of purified affection, she lifts her voice in prayer to Heaven itself. She asks not for vengeance against the man who broke his promises to her, but for mercy—that his perjuries, his broken vows, might find forgiveness in the eyes of the divine. And more than this, she prays that the woman who now bears his name might prove worthy of every blessing: that she be both the happiest and the best of wives, wanting for nothing in the union that was denied to the speaker herself.

In a final act of selfless devotion, she directs her wishes entirely toward his welfare. Let every joy that life can offer, every happiness that fortune might bestow, fall upon Strephon alone—she asks nothing for herself in return, save one small mercy: that he might, in some quiet unguarded moment, spare a thought for her. And so she turns, at last, to address the bride directly—the woman who has won what the speaker could not keep, the victor in love's uncertain contest—offering her words not in bitterness, but in the resigned grace of one who has surrendered all claim except the claim of memory.
outputs.L4:
# The Renunciation

The candles have long since been extinguished, and still she sits with the letter unsent upon her writing desk, its ink dried these three days past. Strephon is married. The words arrived first as gossip carried by a neighbor's careless tongue, then confirmed by the church bells themselves, ringing out across the valley in a peal she once imagined might sound for her own wedding day.

She does not curse him. This is perhaps the strangest thing—that grief of such magnitude should arrive without its customary companion of rage. She had expected, in the private theater of her imagination, that betrayal would summon fury, that she might rail against fickle hearts and broken vows. Instead there is only this quiet, aching hollowness, and beneath it, stubbornly persistent, love itself—unaltered, unashamed, refusing to transform into something bitter simply because circumstance demands it.

The bride, she tells herself, is not the author of this sorrow. A young woman, innocent perhaps of the depth of feeling she has stepped into the middle of, cannot be blamed for accepting what was freely offered to her. Strephon chose, and choices have their reasons, known fully only to the heart that makes them. To hate the new wife would be to compound one injustice with another, and this the speaker will not do. Instead, in the poem's central turn, she offers something far more radical than resentment: she offers blessing.

*May you find joy*, she writes, or thinks, or breathes into the silence of her chamber, *may your years together be long and your affections steady. May children come to fill your house with laughter, and may you never know the particular ache of watching happiness belong to someone else.*

This is not resignation born of weakness but a kind of fierce, quiet strength—the decision to release her claim not because her love has diminished but because love, in its truest form, seeks the beloved's happiness above its own satisfaction. She renounces not her feelings but her right to them, understanding that to hold Strephon in her heart is not a crime, but to demand his heart in return, now that he belongs elsewhere, would be.

And yet she does not ask for nothing. In the poem's final, devastating request, she asks only this: that sometimes, perhaps when autumn light falls a certain way, or when a particular song is played, he might remember her—not with guilt, not with longing that betrays his new vows, but with the simple acknowledgment that she existed, that she loved him, that somewhere her heart continues to beat in rhythm with memories he may have folded away but surely has not entirely forgotten.

The poem closes not with resolution but with a kind of suspended grace—grief transformed not into healing, for that will come slower and separately, but into an act of profound dignity. She has taken the rawest material of heartbreak and shaped from it something luminous: proof that love, even unrequited, even abandoned, can choose generosity over despair, can bless what it cannot possess, and can ask, in its final humility, only to be remembered rather than returned to.
outputs.L5:
# Love, Mine, But

Love is a strange possession—the only kind of "mine" that grows richer the more it's shared. I call you mine, not because I own you, but because something in me recognizes something in you, and in that recognition, a bond forms that language struggles to name. *Mine* becomes less about ownership and more about belonging—a mutual claiming that neither diminishes nor confines.

But love is never simple. It arrives wrapped in contradictions. I want you close, *but* I want you free. I want to protect you, *but* I know you must sometimes fall to learn how to rise. Love says "I am yours," *but* it also demands that we remain, stubbornly, ourselves.

Perhaps this is the paradox at love's core: to say "mine" is to risk everything, *but* to withhold that word is to risk never truly loving at all. We reach for certainty in a feeling that thrives on vulnerability. We want guarantees, *but* love offers none—only the present moment, and the choice, again and again, to stay.

In the end, love may be less a noun than a verb wearing noun's clothing. Not "mine" as a fixed fact, *but* "mine" as an ongoing choice—renewed each day, each conversation, each small act of care. And maybe that's what makes it precious: not that it's guaranteed, *but* that despite all uncertainty, we choose it still.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Restoration-era style poem in heroic couplets about a woman mourning her lost love, who has just married another woman, using pastoral names like "Strephon."
counterfactuals.output:
**Strephon's Inconstancy: A Pastoral Complaint**

Where poplars shade the stream that once was ours,
And violets weep beneath the bridal bow'rs,
I stood and watched the rites I could not stay,
While false-tongued Strephon gave his hand away.
The pipes that sang our love in softer years
Now scorn my sighs and mock my falling tears;
The shepherds dance where once we used to rove,
And strew with flowers the altar of his love—

Not mine, alas, who fondly deemed it mine,
When first he swore by every rural shrine.
He took my hand beneath the trysting tree,
And called the stars to witness constancy;
He said no nymph should ever share his heart,
Till death, unkind, should force our souls apart.
Now Amaryllis wears the ring he gave,
And I am left to weep beside his grave—

His grave of honor, faith, and plighted truth,
Buried too soon beneath the flowers of youth.
Ye gentle swains, who knew my former joy,
Tell me what art has won so fair a boy?
What newer grace has Amaryllis shown,
That was not once believed to be my own?
Perhaps her flocks are more, her fields more wide,
And gold, not love, has made her Strephon's bride.

If so, ye powers, let me no more complain,
For hearts are bought and sold like sheep for gain.
Yet still I'll wander where the myrtles grow,
And tell the echoing groves my tale of woe,
Till pitying Pan, who once loved Syrinx well,
Shall in my note his own misfortune tell;
And when I die, let this my tombstone say:
*"Here lies the maid whom Strephon's vows betrayed;*

*She loved too well, too soon believed him true—
Let this, ye nymphs, a warning be to you."*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dramatic monologue in the voice of a jilted lover addressing her former beloved on his wedding day, written in 17th-century English verse style with rhyming couplets.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Forsaken Mistress's Lament, Upon the Wedding-Day of Her Inconstant Love**

Even now, whilst bells in brazen triumph ring,
And thou dost kneel to wed another spring,
I stand without, in shadow of the door,
A ghost of what thou swor'st to love before.
The organ swells with holy, mocking sound,
While in my breast a thousand griefs are bound.
Didst thou not vow, beneath the harvest moon,
That I alone should be thy bride, and soon?
Didst thou not press thy lips upon my hand
And swear no priest nor kirk should this withstand?
Now priest and kirk have won what I have lost,
And all my love is counted as small cost.

Look how she comes, in silk and virgin white,
Unknowing of the vows thou broke by night—
She knows thee not as I have known thee, sir,
Nor guessed what oaths did once to me refer.
Poor soul, she takes a hand still warm with lies,
And reads no falsehood in thy tender eyes.
I do not curse her, for she knows no sin;
'Tis thou, false heart, that let deception in.

I gave thee all a maid has power to give—
My youth, my faith, the years I meant to live
All folded in thy keeping, as a rose
Is folded till the frost of winter goes.
Thou took'st the bloom and cast the stem aside,
And now dost pluck a fresher, gaudier bride.

Yet mark me, love—for love I still must call
This wound that bleeds beneath my funeral pall—
The stars that heard thy promise shall not sleep;
They kept the record heaven means to keep.
And when the candle of this joy burns thin,
And age creeps cold beneath thy borrowed skin,
Some night thou'lt wake and hear, past reason's door,
My voice, that loved thee truly, and no more.

Go, take thy vows—I'll not defile this day
With curses that would but corrupt my clay.
I'll turn and walk into the world alone,
And leave thee to a joy that's not thine own,
For joy built high on broken faith must fall,
And I shall live to see it, first and last of all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a poignant love poem imitating Aphra Behn's style, where the speaker renounces her claim to a man who has married someone else, yet still secretly loves him?
counterfactuals.output:
**On His Marriage to Another**

Take her, since Fate and thou hast so decreed,
And let my heart be witness that I yield;
Though every vow was writ that I might bleed,
I'll not contest what Hymen's hand hath sealed.

I had thee once in fancy's tender reign,
When every look thou gav'st me was mine own;
Now duty bids me quit the sweet, sweet pain,
And leave thee to a bliss I have not known.

Go, take the hand that innocence hath blessed,
And may she never guess what I have lost;
Let her not read the sorrow in my breast,
Nor know at what a price her joy was bought.

Yet think not, Love, that I have ceased to burn,
Though I have veiled the flame in colder art;
'Tis but the outward face that learns to turn—
Thou keep'st the same soft empire in my heart.

I'll smile upon thee when we chance to meet,
And call thee brother with a steady tongue,
While underneath, in silence too complete,
The old wound bleeds where once thy praises hung.

Oh, cruel Virtue, that commands me thus
To give the substance while I keep the shade!
I lose the man, yet still the passion does
Pursue the ghost that constancy hath made.

Live happy, then, and never know the cost
That bought thy peace with my tormented years;
I ask no more, since all I loved is lost,
But secret leave to shed my private tears.

For though before the world I do resign,
And call another blest in what was mine,
Deep in my soul, where no eye else can see,
Thou'rt wed to her, but true—forever—still to me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem about heartbreak and selfless love, where the narrator wishes happiness upon her rival and the man who betrayed her, using archaic English diction and iambic pentameter couplets.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Blessing Freely Given**

Though thou didst break the vessel of my heart,
And bid farewell, and torn my world apart,
I curse thee not, nor wish thee ill design,
But pray sweet Fortune's hand shall e'er be thine.

She who now holds the hand I once did hold,
Whose eyes have caught the love that hath grown cold—
I hate her not, though jealousy might rise,
For she did naught but love thee with her eyes.

'Tis not her fault that thou didst turn from me,
Nor mine to curse what fate did so decree.
So let her keep thee warm through winter's night,
And may your morrows all be filled with light.

Though I do weep upon my lonely bed,
And mourn the vows that once between us said,
I would not have thee suffer for my pain,
Nor wish upon thy house the bitter rain.

Go forth, and love her well, as once loved me,
Forget the maid who wept beneath yon tree.
I ask but this: that thou shouldst both be blessed,
That in her arms thy weary heart find rest.

For love, when true, doth ask for naught in turn,
But only that the ones we love not burn.
So here I stand, though broken, still I give
My blessing free, that thou and she may live

In joy unmarred by shadows of my grief,
In days made long, in love that finds relief.
Though mine own heart lies shattered on the floor,
I wish thee well—and love thee nevermore.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical piece in the voice of a woman forced to give up her lover to his new bride, expressing grief, hidden passion, and blessings for his marriage, styled after 18th-century amatory poetry.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Bride's Rival: A Farewell

*Being the lament of one who loved before, in the style of the last century's tender muse*

---

I.

Go, then—and let the sacred altar bind
What fate decrees my heart must leave behind.
I will not weep where holy vows are said,
Nor cast a shadow on the bridal bed.
Though every word the priest shall speak for thee
Falls like a small, sweet death reserved for me.

II.

They dress her now in white and orange-flower,
Unknowing of our stolen, secret hour—
When first you swore (ah, swore how tenderly!)
That none should ever love you more than I.
Forgive me, Fate, that I believed it true;
Forgive me, Heart, for loving still, and you.

III.

I'll send no letter, breathe no lover's name,
I'll wear my grief as one might wear no shame—
A private grave wherein my longing lies,
Kept secret even from my open eyes.
By day I'll smile, and speak your bride's name fair;
By night, alone, I'll loose my gathered hair
And let it fall as once it fell for you,
When stars, our only witness, also knew.

IV.

Yet think not, love, I curse this turning tide—
I bless the hour that makes her name thy bride.
May she possess what I could never keep:
Thy waking hours, thy dreaming, and thy sleep.
May she know nothing of the storms that passed
Between us two, too sweet, too bright to last.

V.

I ask no monument, no mournful song,
Only this much—that you'll not think me wrong
To love you still, though silent as the grave,
As faithful as the vow I could not have.
Go, wear the ring, go, speak the sacred vow—
I loved you then. I love you even now.

VI.

So take this blessing, though my voice may break:
May joy attend you for our old love's sake.
May children bless your hearth, may years be kind—
And may you sometimes, only sometimes, mind
That once there was a heart who loved so well,
She let you go, and never once would tell.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
